topic: What if you could catch a shooting star?
title: WHAT IF YOU
COULD CATCH A STAR?

power.rule: you can lock onto a falling shooting star from the ground and slow it to a dead stop in your palm
power.look: catch: time slows as a streak of starlight freezes in your palm with a warm golden-cyan starlight halo, a CATCH HUD chip, and a soft celestial chime

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 0.1 cold open: payoff in the dark park
script.text: Midnight in the park. Freezing air, numb hands. Above the trees, a bright streak of light slashes across the dark. You do not make a wish. You just reach up. Catch.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 0.2 cold open: frozen streak in palm + escalation montage
script.text: Time stutters. The falling streak freezes right in your open palm, humming like a living ember. Warm golden light spills between your mittens. Soon your jars are glowing with starlight, a queue stretches round the block, sirens wail, and the clouds turn blood red.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 0.3 title card
script.text: What if you could catch a star?

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 1.1 chapter card + discovering the power
script.text: Chapter One. The First Catch. It starts on a quiet night in early November, as the Northern Taurids build toward their peak around November twelfth. You are walking home through the park, breath misting in the cold. A shooting star flashes overhead. Just for a laugh, you point your mitten at the sky and close your fingers. Catch.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 1.2 warm hands and bedroom nightlight jar
script.text: A soft chime rings out. Down drops a glowing golden pebble, landing gently in your palm. It does not burn. It feels like a warm marshmallow. You slip it into your pocket, and the walk home feels like summer. Back in your bedroom, you pluck another streak through the window and drop it into an empty jam jar on your nightstand. Instant nightlight.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 1.3 warming cocoa + Mo spots it through the window
script.text: At your desk, a captured star keeps your mug of cocoa piping hot while you work. You think you have found the ultimate cosy life hack. Until you look at the window and see your mate Mo staring through the glass.

script.speaker: mo
script.beat: 1.4 Mo reacts at the window (cliffhanger into Ch 2)
script.text: Wait. Those fall out of the sky for free, and you are using them to warm up cocoa?

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 2.1 chapter card + Mo sets up the stall
script.text: Chapter Two. Wishes for Sale. By the next evening, Mo has turned your secret into a business. He sets up a folding table by the park gate, strings up lights, and tapes a cardboard sign to the front: Genuine Shooting Stars, Hold Your Own Wish. You stand behind the table with empty mason jars, plucking streaks out of the sky on demand. Catch. Catch. Each one lands with a golden chime.

script.speaker: mo
script.beat: 2.2 Mo pitches to the crowd
script.text: Step right up! Fresh off the cosmos! Make a wish while it is still warm, no refunds!

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 2.3 silly wishes and queue round the block
script.text: At first, it is silly fun. A nervous teenager holds a glowing jar and wishes to pass his driving test. A kid wishes for a puppy. Your pockets fill with cash, and the queue stretches round the block.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 2.4 things turn uncomfortable + humming jars (cliffhanger into Ch 3)
script.text: Then the mood turns ugly. People in fancy coats shove to the front, waving money and demanding brighter stars. Customers storm back, furious that their selfish wishes have not come true. Someone tries to smash a jar open on the path. Inside the glass, the captured stars pulse faster, humming with a low vibration that makes your teeth ache. Because what you are catching is not fairy dust at all.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 3.1 chapter card + sand to pebble size
script.text: Chapter Three. The Real Science. Let us pause the chaos and look at what a shooting star really is. When you see a streak of light in the night sky, it is not a giant cartoon star. It is a meteoroid. And most visible meteors come from particles sand grain to pebble sized. That is real.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 3.2 altitude: 80 to 120 km in mesosphere/lower thermosphere
script.text: Even weirder, they are nowhere near the trees. Most meteors burn up roughly eighty to one hundred and twenty kilometres above the ground, high in the mesosphere and lower thermosphere. That is real.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 3.3 speed (27 km/s) and ionised air plasma glow
script.text: So how can a tiny pebble eighty kilometres up shine brightly enough to see from the park? Speed. Taurid meteoroids enter the atmosphere at about twenty seven kilometres per second. That is real. And at twenty seven kilometres per second, the rock is not on fire like wood. Instead, the air around the meteoroid is heated and ionised into a glowing trail of plasma. The glow is mostly superheated air.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 3.4 impossible catch + hand-wave power mechanics & consequences
script.text: Catching a pebble at that speed should be completely impossible. Your power works by locking onto a meteoroid from below and slowing it to a dead stop in your palm. Which raises a big question. Where does all that stopped energy go? Into the jar. And what happens when you reach for something bigger?

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 4.1 chapter card + greedy for a Taurid fireball on the roof
script.text: Chapter Four. Bigger Fish. Alongside tiny dust grains, the Taurids are famous for bright fireballs, made by much larger chunks of rock. Late that night, you climb onto the rooftop above the city. Glowing jars line the wall, humming in the dark. Pebbles feel too small now. You want a real prize. Suddenly, a brilliant green and gold fireball blazes across the clouds, lighting up the whole street. Mo grabs your sleeve.

script.speaker: mo
script.beat: 4.2 Mo warns you
script.text: Leave that one alone, mate! Look at the trail on it! That thing looks angry!

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 4.3 catching the fireball + shockwave + radar
script.text: You reach up anyway. Catch. The sky flashes white. A shockwave rolls across the roof, popping every bulb on the string lights. The fireball slams to a stop above your mittens, shrinking into a sputtering core of blinding plasma. Every car alarm on the street goes off. Because when a bright fireball vanishes mid flight on weather radar and satellite cameras, the world notices.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 4.4 scientists, news vans, and government suits knock (cliffhanger into Ch 5)
script.text: By morning, news vans block your street, scientists with sensors surround the park, and government agents in dark suits knock on your door. They are not here to arrest you. Their telescopes just spotted something else.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 5.1 chapter card + briefing room threat
script.text: Chapter Five. Something Much Bigger. Inside a briefing room, the agents turn a radar screen toward you. Hidden inside the Taurid stream is a dark, house sized object hurtling toward Earth at twenty seven kilometres per second, right on course for the city. There is no time to evacuate, and nothing else can stop it. So the world asks you to stand in the park and catch it.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 5.2 dark city tension + Mo stands by you
script.text: That night, the city cuts every light. Searchlights sweep the clouds. Scientists watch from behind shields. Mo stands beside you on the path, knees shaking.

script.speaker: mo
script.beat: 5.3 Mo nervous joke
script.text: No pressure or anything. Just the whole city behind us. Use both hands, yeah?

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 5.4 the giant bolide enters + the attempt (cliffhanger into Ch 6)
script.text: High above, roughly one hundred kilometres up, the clouds turn blood red. A deep roar shakes the ground as a colossal fireball tears through the upper air, dragging a tail of plasma across the sky. You plant your feet, raise both hands toward the glare, and whisper the word. Catch. A shockwave flattens the grass. The roar drops into silence. Slowly, impossibly, the giant fireball halts just above your fingertips. And as the plasma clears, your breath catches.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 6.1 chapter card + the plasma clears to reveal the craft
script.text: Chapter Six. What You Caught. The superheated air fades into the night breeze, and you finally see what is hovering above your palms. It is not a jagged space rock. Its surface is smooth dark metal, shaped into clean geometric panels that glint in the moonlight, etched with glowing cyan symbols no human ever wrote.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 6.2 all the jars pulse in sync — beacons
script.text: Behind you, every mason jar you filled all week suddenly flares bright blue. All those tiny pebbles pulse in the exact same rhythm, answering the craft above your hands. They were never random grains of space dust. They were beacons, sent ahead to find someone who could catch them.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 6.3 the hatch opens + closing question
script.text: And now that you have caught their ship, a hatch on its underside clicks open. If you could catch a falling star tonight, and it answered back, would you open your hand, or let it go?

science.claim: Taurid meteoroids enter at about 27 km/s.
science.working: Southern Taurid (STA) meteoroids enter Earth's atmosphere at about 27 km/s (Northern Taurids, NTA, enter at about 29 km/s).
science.source: International Meteor Organization (IMO) Meteor Shower Outlook / Calendar (STA: 27 km/s, NTA: 29 km/s)

science.claim: Most meteors burn up roughly 80-120 km above the ground (mesosphere / lower thermosphere).
science.working: Meteors become visible and ablate primarily between 80 km and 120 km altitude (around 100 km sits right in this mesosphere / lower thermosphere band).
science.source: NASA / American Meteor Society (AMS) Meteor FAQ

science.claim: Most visible meteors come from particles sand-grain to pebble sized.
science.working: The vast majority of visible shooting stars are produced by meteoroids ranging in size from a grain of sand to a small pebble (millimetres to a few centimetres across), while brighter fireballs come from larger fragments.

science.claim: The Northern Taurids peak around 12 Nov 2026, and the Taurids are known for bright fireballs.
science.working: The Northern Taurid meteor shower peaks around 12 November 2026 (following the Southern Taurids in early November), and both branches are noted by NASA and the IMO for producing bright fireballs.
science.source: NASA "What's Up: November 2026" & IMO Meteor Shower Outlook

science.claim: The glow of a meteor is mostly the air around the meteoroid being heated and ionised into plasma, not the rock burning like wood on fire.
science.working: At hypersonic entry speeds (~27 km/s), ram pressure compresses and heats the air ahead of the meteoroid to thousands of kelvins, ionising the surrounding atmospheric gas and ablated vapour into a glowing plasma trail.
science.source: NASA / American Meteor Society (AMS) Meteor FAQ
